data.title: Navbar
data.tagline: Keep the brand, main destinations, and key action easy to reach
data.description: A website navbar helps visitors understand where they can go and how to return home. Keep the number of primary links manageable, show the current section when useful, and adapt the menu for smaller screens without hiding essential paths.

distinctions.label: Header
distinctions.explanation: Header is the complete top page area and can include brand, search, and sign-in. Navbar is the portion dedicated to primary navigation.

use: Access to sign in or a key action
A compact menu that remains consistent across pages
avoid: Put every page in the top row
Use labels that change between pages
Hide important links only in a desktop hover menu
Let a sticky navbar cover the content below

lessonPractice.title: Product, Templates, Pricing, and Blog must stay consistent across the site and show the current section. Where should they go?

options.label: Place them in a global top navbar and highlight the current section
options.feedback: These are major cross-page destinations, so a persistent navbar provides stable access and location.

options.label: Create a separate set of content tabs on every page
options.feedback: Tabs organize peer content within one page or object, not the site's main destinations.

options.label: Hide them in a right drawer by default on desktop
options.feedback: Hiding every core destination despite available space adds steps and weakens location awareness.

data.agentPrompt: Use one consistent top navbar for Product, Templates, Pricing, and Blog across the site and highlight the current section. Verify destinations, focus, sticky overlap, and opening and closing the mobile menu.

references.title: Mega Menus Work Well for Site Navigation
